title: Deployment strategy decision aid - SME FinOps and latency tradeoffs
content:
Summary:
This is a short decision aid for an SME customer POC where the primary product constraint is aggressive per-request latency (95th percentile target <= 120ms) while procurement requires strong FinOps controls. The goal: recommend a deployment pattern (hosted, dedicated, private, or hybrid) that balances cost predictability, latency SLOs, and an easy escalation path from POC -> production.

Context and customer profile:
- Industry: vertical SaaS serving accounting/financial workflows for small-to-mid enterprises.
- Data sensitivity: mixed — most traffic is non-sensitive, but some routes (tax ID, payroll) are regulated and must be restricted to customer-owned infrastructure or VPC peers.
- Traffic profile for POC: bursty during business hours, quiet nights. Expected 500–2,000 requests/day; peak QPS ~ 0.5–2.
- Cost sensitivity: CFO asks for predictable monthly spend, prefers reserved commitments over unpredictable overage.
- Timeline: 8-week POC, move to pilot within 3 months if latency & accuracy targets met.

Objectives (POC-level):
- Demonstrate 95th percentile latency <= 120ms for primary generative route under representative load.
- Show clear unit cost to operations team and an ops playbook for scaling.
- Validate data-path isolation for regulated routes.
- Produce a FinOps model (TCO) for hosted vs dedicated vs private across 6/12/24 month horizons.

Constraints and non-goals:
- Non-goal: building custom model training pipelines — only serving inference.
- Regulatory constraint: regulated routes must not traverse multi-tenant shared GPUs (unless encrypted & contractually isolated).
- Limited infra team bandwidth at customer — prefer Redwood-managed options where possible.

Decision criteria (ranked):
1) Latency predictability (weight 35%) — measured P95 under realistic prompts.
2) Cost predictability (weight 30%) — ability to forecast monthly spend and cap risk.
3) Implementation effort (weight 15%) — time to first successful endpoint and runbooks.
4) Data isolation / compliance (weight 12%) — meets customer regulatory needs.
5) Operational control & observability (weight 8%) — RBAC, logs, tracing.

Option assessments (short):
- Hosted API (Redwood-hosted):
  Pros: fastest time-to-value, zero infra for customer, built-in autoscaling and observability, good for non-sensitive routes. Pricing per-token keeps up-front low.
  Cons: per-token variability, possible P95 spikes during noisy neighbors if not using dedicated lanes. For regulated routes, requires encryption + contractual agreements; may not satisfy customer for certain PIIs.
  P95 latency expectation (typical): 60–200ms depending on model/sequence; can meet 120ms if model is small and request size short and if customer accepts hosted SLA.

- Dedicated capacity (reserved Redwood capacity):
  Pros: predictable throughput and latency, predictable monthly invoice (reserved commitment), better isolation than shared hosted. Good middle-ground for FinOps.
  Cons: higher baseline cost, requires commitment sizing; bursting strategy must be explicit (burst buckets or autoscale policies).
  P95 latency expectation: 40–90ms for common gen model families on reserved GPUs with tuning.

- Private deployment (customer VPC / on-prem):
  Pros: maximum data control, full network isolation, can be required for regulated routes. Latency to customer app lowest if co-located.
  Cons: highest setup cost, involves ops at customer, longer lead time, makes FinOps less predictable unless customer owns hardware. Maintenance and upgrades are heavier.
  P95 latency expectation: 20–60ms if co-located and properly sized.

Recommended pattern for this customer (POC -> Pilot): hybrid split-by-route, phased rollout
- Phase 0 (PoC week 0–2): Hosted-first for non-sensitive routes + minimal dedicated pool reserved for gen-primary workload tests. Purpose: fastest validation of latency targets and functional correctness.
  - Create hosted endpoints for 75% of routes (non-PII). Use Redwood streaming to measure tail latencies.
  - Reserve a 1-node dedicated pool (small GPU) for synthetic load runs against the same model to establish deterministic P95 baseline.

- Phase 1 (POC week 2–6): Introduce split routing at API-layer (route-based policy): non-sensitive -> hosted; regulated routes -> private/VPC peered deployment or dedicated lanes depending on compliance acceptance.
  - If customer required private for regulated routes, provision a VPC-private deployment for those specific endpoints only (minimum surface area). Otherwise, push regulated routes to dedicated-only lanes with contractual isolation.
  - Collect cost telemetry and parameterize FinOps model. Run stress tests to validate autoscale and burst behaviors.

- Phase 2 (Pilot month 3+): Move to dedicated-first for predictable monthly billing while leaving non-critical low-volume routes on hosted to save costs. Prepare for eventual customer-owned private deployment for regulated workloads if procurement requests.

Topology notes and fallbacks:
- Routing policy: implement request routing that selects backend by (route sensitivity, latency SLA, cost tier). Example: sensitive && P95 target < 100ms -> private; sensitive && low traffic -> dedicated lane; otherwise hosted.
- Fallback behavior: if dedicated capacity exhausted, failover to hosted non-sensitive variant (caveat: ensure no regulated data routes failover into non-compliant backend).
- Caching / prefix-KV: enable prefix caching on the hosted routes to reduce cost and improve P95 for repeated prompts.

FinOps modeling assumptions (for POC):
- Hosted: $ per 1k tokens = X (make transparent in customer deck; we'll plug real numbers).
- Dedicated: monthly reserved node = Y; assume 1.5x utilization to meet peaks.
- Private on-prem: one-time setup + monthly ops estimate Z.
- Sensitivity table to include: 50% utilization vs 80% utilization.

Validation plan & SLOs:
- Instrument: P95 latency per route, token consumption per route, error rate, cold-start latency metric.
- Test harness: use real prompt set from product team (sanitized) and synthetic spikes (2x expected peak) for stress testing.
- Acceptance criteria (POC success): P95 <= 120ms on primary route under 2x expected QPS; cost per 1k tokens under X threshold for projected monthly usage; documented ops runbook.

Operational runbook (high level):
- On-call playbook: steps to scale dedicated pool, how to temporarily throttle hosted clients, and how to enable fallback.
- Rollout checklist: smoke test, canary traffic 5% -> 20% -> 100% over 24–72h with rollback windows.
- Observability: dashboards per model/route showing P95, CPU/GPU utilization, token cost, and KV cache hit rate.

Open questions / to resolve with customer:
- Exact procurement constraints around reserved spend vs monthly SaaS. Is a 12-month commit possible? (Impacts dedicated recommendation.)
- Which specific routes are legally required to be private? We need an enumerated list and sample payloads for compliance review.
- Acceptable automatic fallback policies for regulated routes (must be strict deny vs allow with masking?).

Action items (next steps):
- SE: build a 2-week test plan with workload generator and FinOps spreadsheet template (owner: Leah). Target ready by 2025-01-22.
- Infra: provision a 1-node dedicated pool for tests (owner: Marcus). Target ready by 2025-01-20.
- Customer PM: provide sanitized prompt corpus and list of regulated routes (owner: customer).
- Finance: prepare a 6/12/24 month TCO comparing hosted vs dedicated vs private (owner: Priya).

Notes-to-self:
- Keep the private surface area as small as possible to reduce customer ops burden — prefer route-level private endpoints rather than full private cluster.
- Document exact SLAs and contractual isolation language if recommending dedicated lanes for regulated routes.

Appendix (short examples):
- Example routing rule (pseudo):
  if route.labels.contains('pii') then backend = private-vpc-endpoint
  else if monthly_usage_estimate > threshold then backend = dedicated-pool
  else backend = hosted-standard

- Quick cost sensitivity example (placeholder numbers):
  Hosted 6mo: $A
  Dedicated reserved node 6mo: $B (break-even if utilization > 65%)
  Private on-prem 6mo: $C + ops (break-even if sustained high throughput and strict data constraints)

End of doc.
